title: Sebastian and the Portrait
premise: When insurance investigator Rosalind Dunmore receives a confession letter for a drowning death she was hired to rule accidental — postmarked the day after the victim's funeral — she travels to the decaying seaside estate of Wrenmoor to close what should be an open-and-shut fraud. But the letter's details match a case file that was never made public, and the house's inhabitants each seem to know her arrival before she does, as if scripted. Following clues hidden in a centuries-old family portrait and its painted double, Rosalind discovers the confession was written by the killer's twin, who died years ago — meaning someone alive is impersonating a dead man to frame the past. In the climax, at low tide on the mudflats where the body was found, Rosalind traps the killer: the estate's archivist, who forged his own identity decades ago and has been erasing anyone who could expose that he is not the Dunmore heir at all.
about_author: Silas Winterbourne is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent fifteen years cataloguing shipwreck claims and unclaimed inheritances along the English coast. They write mysteries in a drafty house overlooking the same grey tidelands that haunt their fiction.

chapters.title: The Letter That Arrived Late
chapters.summary: Rosalind Dunmore, POV. A confession letter arrives postmarked the day after Edmund Dunmore's funeral, confessing to a drowning Rosalind's firm already ruled accidental. The letter cites case details never made public. Her photographic memory flags one impossible detail: the handwriting matches documents from a man dead eleven years. Beat: cold fascination hardening into obligation.

chapters.title: Wrenmoor at Ebb
chapters.summary: Rosalind arrives at the cliffside estate under cover of assessing the life-insurance claim. The household — widow Maren, brooding nephew Callum, and archivist Tobias Fenwick — each greet her with unsettling familiarity, as though expecting her. She notices the great portrait of the Dunmore patriarch has been recently cleaned. Beat: unease beneath polite ritual.

chapters.title: A Face Painted Twice
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Examining the portrait, she discovers faint pentimento: a second face beneath the patriarch's, subtly different. Cross-referencing estate records, she finds the archive meticulously complete — too complete, every gap smoothed over. Fenwick watches her work with courteous patience. Beat: the first certainty that something has been deliberately erased.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. He takes Rosalind to the mudflats where Edmund drowned, revealing the family's quiet knowledge that Edmund had been investigating their own lineage before his death. He shows her Edmund's hidden notebook, half water-ruined. Beat: grief curdling into suspicion; Callum doesn't know if he's recruiting her or testing her.

chapters.title: The Dead Man's Hand
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She traces the confession letter's paper and ink to materials stocked only in Wrenmoor's own archive. Someone inside wrote it using the hand of Aldous Dunmore, the twin who died in 1989. When she confronts Maren, the widow denies everything but flinches at Aldous's name. Beat: dread replacing confidence.

chapters.title: Inheritance of Lies
chapters.summary: Fenwick's POV, unreliable and controlled. He catalogs the household like specimens, reflecting on how identities are inherited rather than born. He quietly removes a page from Edmund's recovered notebook and burns correspondence in the boiler. Beat: chilling competence; the reader now knows more than Rosalind.

chapters.title: The Second Funeral
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Digging into parish records, she learns Aldous Dunmore's body was never found — only his coat. And the man buried as Aldous in 1989 was identified by Fenwick himself, then a young assistant archivist. The portrait's hidden face, she realizes, is Aldous. Beat: vertigo; the case file itself becomes the crime scene.

chapters.title: Locked Archive
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Fearing exposure of old complicity, Maren warns Rosalind to leave, then is found unconscious at the archive door, drugged. Rosalind realizes the killer is closing ranks: everyone who could confirm or deny Aldous's identity is being silenced. Callum vanishes overnight. Beat: isolation and rising panic.

chapters.title: Low Water
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Using the tide tables from Edmund's notebook, she predicts when the mudflats will give up what they took — Edmund's missing satchel — and stages a public search to force the killer's hand. Fenwick comes to destroy it, and she springs the trap, confronting him with the forged burial record and the portrait's second face. Beat: tense, cold-blooded climax.

chapters.title: The Portrait Restored
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, weeks later. Fenwick — revealed as no Dunmore at all, a foundling who stole Aldous's identity as a boy and killed to keep it — confesses fully. Conservators uncover the true portrait: two brothers, painted together. Rosalind closes the file, but keeps Edmund's notebook, understanding at last that belonging can't be archived. Beat: melancholy resolution and earned peace.
